There are 6 learning principles that improve efficiency�

  1. established sets increase awareness.�
  2. a conscious intent to learn increases memory.
  3. accuracy of our memory is governed by the nature of the stimulus.�

Principle 1: Established sets increase awareness.�

Memory is improved if learners establish a set prior to beginning a task involving memorization.

Set refers�to mental readiness. It tells learners to be aware of specific aspects of the material. If you are told in advance to  look for something in a reading or a film or a lesson, your mind is receptive to the appearance of this information.

Principle 2: Memory is facilitated by the conscious intent to learn.

If you decide you are determined to concentrate and not be distracted, you have a better chance of making this happen.�

It s amazing what you can remember when you tell yourself,  I must remember this information.

Principle 3: The accuracy of our memory is governed by the nature of the stimulus.�

Organized material is more easily handled by the memory system than is disorganized information.

Advanced organizers�- brief packages of information that are presented before the main content  are sometimes used to assist learners. Tables of Contents in text books are one example of an advanced organizer. The Scene Summary before the actual text of a scene in a Shakespearean play is another example.�By reading that before delving into the scene, learners are better able to grasp what is happening.The  blurb on the back covers of books and DVD cases is yet another type of advanced organizer.

Principle 4: Distributed practice is more�effective for learning than is massed practice.�

Periodic reviews of material reinforce memory.�Soon after the initial exposure to the data, a review should be given.�In most cases, frequent review periods of shorter duration are better for learning than one long review.

(This is why you may not remember information you crammed into your brain before an exam by the time you start the next unit or course.�If you reviewed every day for a week before the test, you would have anchored the material more firmly in your mind.) This can be avoided with distributed study periods well in advance of the exam.

Principle 5: Self-recitation increases the retention of information.�

Recitation demands the learner s full attention.�It makes the learner an active participant in�the learning process�and in the selection of what will be remembered. Saying out loud or writing down what you want to learn or remember is self-recitation.� Remember learning your times tables in grade three?� You probably repeated and repeated and repeated them over and over and over again until you knew them backwards and forwards.� That's self-recitation.�


Principle 6: Emotions are an important agent in what is remembered or forgotten.

Generally, learning is more�effective in a pleasant, relaxed atmosphere. Sometimes, however, a bit of tension can cause the learner to be  on their toes and ready to learn. When a student anticipates what might happen next in a class - the outcome of a science experiment, or the ending of a book the class is reading, for example - learning may more readily take place. Too much tension in the learning environment, though, may lead to the learner  freezing up and being unable to learn anything. For example, a student began having frequent nightmares about his Math teacher.�The dreams were so vivid and graphic, that he couldn t concentrate in Math class, and he was paralyzed by fear of the teacher.�His grades began to suffer, so he withdrew and took the class online.
